## Review: Habits tracker

I read the actual source (not just task titles): `dates.ts`/`streaks.ts` (streak math), `db.ts` (IndexedDB persistence), `state.ts` (the app's data flow), `App.tsx`, `HabitDialog.tsx`, `ImportDialog.tsx`, `backup.ts`, `vite.config.ts`/`main.tsx` (offline), `styles.css`, the test files, and compared a rendered sketch screenshot against the built CSS/markup. Everything the owner was promised is genuinely implemented, not stubbed.

**What stood out positively:** the date/streak logic is unusually well-tested — `dates.test.ts` explicitly checks leap-year rollovers (2024-02-29) and DST transitions in Europe/Berlin and America/New_York by swapping `process.env.TZ`, plus a 400-day no-repeat walk across four time zones. `streaks.ts` correctly treats an un-ticked "today" as not yet breaking yesterday's streak. Import requires a confirmation dialog stating it replaces everything, matching the agreed decision. The habit-name-tap-to-select-heatmap behavior persists via `localStorage`, also as agreed.

**One real nuance for the owner to know:** on phone-width screens (≤560px), CSS hides the inline 7-day strip on each habit row (`.spark { display: none; }` in the mobile media query). On a phone, ticking a past day only works through the "Catch up" block below, not directly on the row. This is actually the documented reason the catch-up day-chips exist, so it's intentional — but it means the promised "seven-day strip is tappable" screen element is a desktop-only affordance, not something you'll see on your phone.

All automated checks (install, typecheck, 45+ unit tests, production build) passed on every run, including the final offline/service-worker task.

The work is solid: pure logic extracted into testable modules (`habits.ts`, `backup.ts`), both covered by real unit tests, native `<dialog>` used correctly for modals with sensible Escape/backdrop semantics, and the author caught and fixed a genuine stale-closure data-loss bug (`renameHabit`+`recolorHabit` chained together silently reverting one field) by introducing `updateHabit`. PWA setup is standard and gated to prod only, so dev/test are unaffected. Footbar now matches the sketch in full, satisfying the phase goal.

Two non-blocking things worth tracking for later, not worth a rework cycle:

It was fixed for the one combination that was hit, but two of these fired close together (e.g. rapid double-click on reorder arrows) could still race. Worth hardening if Phase 3 adds more concurrent-mutation UI.
- `HabitDialog` and `ImportDialog` duplicate the same `showModal`/`close`/backdrop-click boilerplate; a shared hook would remove the duplication.

None of these threaten correctness today or block building on this phase.

The phase holds together well. The correctness-critical logic (date arithmetic, streaks, IndexedDB persistence) is thoroughly unit-tested including leap years, DST transitions, and month/year boundaries — exactly the areas the brief flagged as important. The optimistic-update-with-rollback pattern in `toggle` satisfies "instant tick, no data loss," and the author caught and fixed a genuine hit-area overlap bug in the 7-day spark strip through actual interactive verification (Playwright) rather than assumption. Screenshots confirm the Today screen renders correctly at both viewport sizes with no overflow, matching the sketch structure (topbar → progress → rows → catch-up → heatmap).

A few non-blocking gaps worth carrying into the next phase:
- `createHabit` in `db.ts` computes `order` via read-then-write (list all, then max+1) with no atomicity — fine today since nothing calls it concurrently, but will race once an "add habit" UI or import feature calls it without serializing.
- `renameHabit`, `recolorHabit`, `setArchived`, `reorder`, `addHabit` in `state.ts` update local state before the DB write but, unlike `toggle`, have no rollback if the write rejects. Not exercised yet (no UI wires to them), but should get the same rollback treatment when that UI lands.
- `Heat.tsx` maps over `weeks`/cells without `key` props — harmless today since the list never reorders, but worth fixing for hygiene.
- No jsdom/testing-library is installed, so the interactive behaviors (mount loading, reload persistence, rollback) have no automated regression test — only manual Playwright verification. Reasonable for Phase 1, but later phases adding habit management UI will want a DOM test setup rather than relying on manual re-verification each time.
- `deleteHabit` in `db.ts` is dead code (no caller) — low priority, trim or keep for the eventual archive/delete UI.

Reviewing against the prior rework feedback and the plan's own criteria.

**Prior issue — resolved.** The previous rework flagged a mismatch: the owner-facing text promised fixing "any of the last seven days" but only yesterday was buildable. This revision fixes it on both fronts — p1-today-screen's row strip is now interactive for all 7 days (point 4) and the catch-up block now uses day chips covering all 7 days with "Today" included (point 5), and `p1-state`'s `isEditableDay`/`toggle` window is explicitly today‑6..today. The outcome text, feature bullets, and task acceptance criteria are now internally consistent.

**Scope and structure.** M/low-risk is honest — new standalone app, no existing system to protect, UI-heavy. Two phases is right-sized for this scope (real data + tested core logic first, then management/export/offline). Dependency chain is strictly linear and sound (setup → dates → store → state → today-screen → habit-editor → export/import → offline), and tooling is bootstrapped in the first task so every later task's verify commands are runnable from the start.

**Testing discipline.** Matches the tiered-test guidance well: per-task verify commands are scoped to the touched test file (`npm test -- src/lib/dates.test.ts src/lib/streaks.test.ts`, etc.), with the full suite reserved for the two phase gates. The date/streak test list (leap year, DST transitions, month/year boundaries, a 400-day no-repeat walk) is the right level of rigor for the brief's correctness requirement.

**Model/effort allocation** is sensible: `sonnet/high` on the correctness-critical date/streak logic and the large UI build, `sonnet/low` on the mechanical offline/PWA setup.

**Minor, non-blocking note for the feedback log:** `p1-store`'s `deleteHabit` (with its own transactional tick-cleanup and test) appears to have no caller anywhere in the plan — archiving uses `setArchived`, not deletion. Not a defect, just a bit of persistence surface the app never exercises; worth trimmin

Addressed: the brief does ask for past days, so rather than trimming the promise I extended `p1-today-screen` to actually build a full week of catch-up — the 7-day spark cells become tap targets on desktop, and the catch-up block gains a day-chip selector (defaulting to yesterday) so the same editing works at 375 px, where the spark is hidden. Acceptance criteria now check both paths, and the heatmap staying read-only is recorded as an open question.

I reviewed the plan against the brief, the sketch-derived outcome description, and the eight task specs.

**What's solid:**
- Scope assessment (M, low risk, 2 phases/8 tasks) is honest — greenfield app, no existing system to break, matches the "standard" medium-job process.
- Tooling is set up in the very first task (`p1-setup`), so every subsequent task's verify commands are runnable from the start.
- Test tiering matches the global CLAUDE.md guidance well: per-task verify runs filtered test files (e.g. `npm test -- src/lib/dates.test.ts`), full suite + build only at each phase gate.
- The two important aspects called out in the brief are both addressed concretely: streak/date correctness gets its own hardened module (`dates.ts` never uses `toISOString`/UTC, explicit leap-year/DST test cases) with a `sonnet/high` model assignment reflecting its risk; "ticking feels instant" is handled by an explicit optimistic-update-then-persist pattern in `p1-state` with rollback on failure.
- Tasks are scoped to single sessions with precise, checkable acceptance criteria, and verify commands genuinely exercise those criteria (dedicated test files per task).
- Dependency chain and phase split are sensible; priority-5 "Daily check-in" ships in phase 1, priority-5 "Habits" CRUD follows immediately in phase 2 — reasonable given this is already a minimal 2-phase plan.

**One concrete problem:** the outcome copy oversells what phase 1 builds. "What the owner gets" states the owner can "fix yesterday or any day in the last week," but every task that implements catch-up (`p1-today-screen`'s "YESTERDAY · CATCH UP" block, and its own bullet list two lines below) only covers **yesterday** — there is no task, acceptance criterion, or UI element anywhere in the plan that lets the owner edit a day further back than yesterday (the 7-day `.spark` strip is explicitly read-only display). This is an internal inconsistency between the plan's own summary and its own task specs, not just a minor copy

Plan below. One thing worth flagging: the sketch hard-coded the bottom heatmap to the first habit and showed only three habits in the "yesterday" block — the plan makes both real (selectable habit, all habits), which is the only place I deviate from the picture, and it's in `open_questions`.

The build is two phases: first the real app end to end (IndexedDB persistence, today's check-in, streaks, heatmap, tested date logic), then habit management, export/import and offline.

Three directions for the main screen, all running on real Preact + Vite with real streak/calendar maths. Switch between them with the tabs in the header (`?d=today|grid|cards`) — that switcher is a sketch device, the real app would ship one.

**Today list** — today's habits as big tap rows, a "x of 5 done" bar on top, a yesterday catch-up block, one heatmap at the bottom.
**Week grid** — habits × last 7 days as a table, tick any cell including past days, streak column at the right, heatmap for the selected habit below. Densest; on the phone the table scrolls sideways so the streak column is off-screen.
**Habit cards** — a card per habit with the tick, current/longest/30-day numbers and its own 6-month heatmap always visible. Most informative, longest page.

The streak and calendar maths is real (local-date `YYYY-MM-DD` keys so time zones and DST can't shift a day, month-boundary and leap-year safe). The data is not: habits and ticks are generated in memory, so a reload resets them — IndexedDB is the real build's job, as are export/import, which are buttons only.
